title: Classification, adaptation and evolution
specPoints: Year 9 bridging: the five kingdoms, the ranks and binomial names, keys, adaptation, natural selection, extinction and biodiversity

tips.title: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup
tips.body: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species: largest to smallest, and the last two make the scientific name. *Homo sapiens* is genus *Homo*, species *sapiens*, genus with a capital, both in italics.

tips.title: Species means fertile offspring
tips.body: If a question mentions a **mule** or a **liger**, it is testing the species definition. The parents can breed, but the offspring is **infertile**, so the parents are separate species. The word to write is *fertile*.

tips.title: Variation before selection
tips.body: Read your natural selection answer and find the sentence where the variation appears. It must come **before** the environment does anything. If your answer says organisms *changed to suit* the environment, rewrite it: the forms already existed, and the environment decided which survived to breed.

tips.title: Feature, what it does, why it helps here
tips.body: Every adaptation answer is three parts: the **feature**, what it **does**, and why that helps **in this habitat**. *Thick fur* is one mark at best; *thick fur traps air, which insulates, so less heat is lost to the Arctic cold* is the full answer.

tips.title: Keys use structure, never colour
tips.body: A key must send every member of a species down the same branch, so it asks about features that do not vary: legs, wings, shells, segments. Colour and size vary within a species and change with age, which is why they are wrong answers when a question asks what makes a good key.

why.matters: There are millions of kinds of living thing, and this topic is how biology copes with that: sort them, name them so that everyone means the same one, and explain why each is built the way it is. The explanation, natural selection, is the biggest idea in the subject, and it runs on one rule: variation first, then the environment chooses. That rule explains a moth on a sooty tree, a bacterium in a hospital that a drug no longer kills, and a dodo. The GCSE unit on evolution adds the evidence and the fossils; this topic gives it the ranks, the names, the key and the four steps.

examples.title: The tiger's Latin name
examples.body: A tiger is a tiger in English, a tigre in French, and a dozen other things in the languages of the countries it lives in. To every scientist it is *Panthera tigris*, and the lion is *Panthera leo*. The shared first word says they sit in the same genus and are close relatives; the different second word says they are different species, which the liger proves: lions and tigers can mate, but the offspring is usually infertile. Linnaeus set up this two-word system in the 1750s so that a name would mean one thing everywhere, and it still does.

visual.alt: A table of three species with their scientific names split into genus and species: the lion and tiger share the genus Panthera, and humans are Homo sapiens

examples.title: The moth that the smoke chose
examples.body: Manchester's peppered moths were pale and speckled, hidden on the lichen of clean bark. A dark one was first recorded in 1848, a rare oddity that birds picked off. Then factory soot blackened the trees, and on dark bark the pale moths were the ones the birds could see. By 1895, 98 of every 100 moths in the city were dark. Not one moth had changed colour; the smoke had changed which colour survived. After the Clean Air Act of 1956 the lichen came back and so did the pale moths, which is the proof that the environment does the choosing.

visual.alt: Two bars to scale: ninety-eight per cent of Manchester's peppered moths were dark in 1895 and two per cent pale, forty-nine dark for every pale one

examples.title: Why the doctor says finish the course
examples.body: A course of antibiotics is a natural-selection experiment you run in your own body. The bacteria vary, and a few happen to carry an allele that lets them survive a little of the drug. Take the whole course and even those die. Stop halfway because you feel better and the survivors are exactly the resistant ones; they breed, and the next person to catch them finds the drug does not work. It is the peppered moth again, with the antibiotic as the bird, and it runs in days.

visual.alt: A flow chart of antibiotic resistance as natural selection: a varied population, the susceptible bacteria die first, and whether the course is finished decides whether the resistant few die or survive to breed

steps.title: Why we classify, and the five kingdoms
steps.body:
There are millions of kinds of living thing, and nobody can learn them one at a time. **Classification** sorts them into groups by the features they share, so that knowing the group tells you a great deal about a member you have never met. Say *mammal* and you have already said warm-blooded, fur, milk for the young.

**The biggest groups are the five kingdoms.**

- **Animals**: many cells, no cell walls, feed on other organisms, most can move about.
- **Plants**: many cells, cell walls of cellulose, chloroplasts, make their own food by photosynthesis.
- **Fungi**: cell walls but no chloroplasts; feed on dead or living material by digesting it outside the cell and absorbing it; yeasts, moulds, mushrooms.
- **Protists**: mostly single cells with a nucleus; amoeba, algae, the malaria parasite.
- **Prokaryotes**: single cells with **no nucleus**; the bacteria.

**Viruses are in none of them.** They are not cells and do not feed, grow or divide on their own, so the five kingdoms leave them out.

The kingdoms were originally sorted by what organisms **look like** and how they feed. Comparing **DNA** has since redrawn some of the lines, and the GCSE unit on evolution explains how that led to a system of three **domains** above the kingdoms. For now, the five kingdoms are the map.

steps.title: From kingdom to species, and the two-part name
steps.body:
A kingdom is far too big to be useful on its own, so each is divided again and again. The ranks, from largest to smallest, are:

**kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**

A phrase to hold the order: *King Philip Came Over For Good Soup*. Each rank down, the group is smaller and its members share more.

**You, all the way down.** Kingdom Animalia; phylum Chordata, animals with a backbone or its forerunner; class Mammalia; order Primates, with the monkeys and apes; family Hominidae, the great apes; genus *Homo*; species *sapiens*.

**A species** is a group whose members can **breed together to produce fertile offspring**. A horse and a donkey can breed, but their offspring, a mule, is infertile, so horse and donkey are separate species. The word *fertile* is the mark.

**The two-part name.** Every species has a scientific name made of its **genus** and its **species**: *Homo sapiens*, *Panthera leo* for the lion, *Panthera tigris* for the tiger. The system is called **binomial naming** and was set out by the Swedish naturalist **Carl Linnaeus** in the **1750s**. The genus takes a capital, the species does not, and the name is in *italics* or underlined. Sharing a genus, as the lion and tiger do, means being close relatives.

**Why a Latin name at all.** The same animal has a different common name in every language and sometimes in every county; the binomial name is the same everywhere, so two scientists always know they mean the same species.

steps.title: Using a key
steps.body:
A **key** identifies an unknown organism by asking a series of questions, each with **two** answers. Each answer either names the organism or sends you to the next question. Because every question splits the possibilities in two, it is called a **dichotomous** key.

**Writing a good key** means choosing features that are **easy to see** and **do not change**: number of legs, wings or not, shell or not. Colour and size are poor choices, because they vary between individuals of the same species and change with age.

**Using one** is a matter of answering honestly and following the arrows, one question at a time, without skipping ahead to the animal you think it is. The flowchart is the key for four small garden animals: an earthworm, a spider, a flea and a ladybird.

visuals.alt: A flow chart used as a key for four garden animals: no legs is an earthworm, legs but not six is a spider, six legs without wings is a flea, and six legs with wings is a ladybird

steps.title: Adaptation
steps.body:
An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an organism **survive and reproduce** in the place it lives. Every organism is a collection of them, and a question about an unfamiliar animal is really asking you to read them off.

**A polar bear** in the Arctic: thick **fur** and a layer of **fat** under the skin to keep warm; **white** fur for camouflage on snow while it hunts; **small ears** so less heat is lost; wide **paws** that spread its weight on ice and paddle in water.

**A camel** in the desert: **fat stored in the hump**, not water, so the rest of the body has little insulation and stays cooler; long **eyelashes** and closing **nostrils** against sand; wide **feet** that do not sink; the ability to lose a lot of water without harm.

**A cactus** in the same desert: leaves reduced to **spines**, so little water is lost and animals are kept off; a thick **stem** that stores water; **shallow, wide roots** that catch rain the moment it falls.

**Two kinds of adaptation.** Fur, spines and humps are **structural**: parts of the body. Hunting at night, hibernating, or a desert fox spending the day in a burrow, are **behavioural**: things the organism does. A full answer usually gives both.

**The habit that earns marks:** name the feature, then say **what it does** and **why that helps here**. *Thick fur* is a feature; *thick fur traps air, which insulates, so less heat is lost to the cold air* is an adaptation.

steps.title: Variation, competition and natural selection: the peppered moth
steps.body:
Organisms are adapted to where they live because of a process that never stops, and it has four steps.

1. Individuals in a species **vary**, because of their different alleles.
2. More are born than can survive, so they **compete**: for food, for space, for mates, and against predators and disease.
3. The ones whose variations suit the conditions best are more likely to **survive and reproduce**.
4. They pass on the alleles for those variations, so in the next generation those variations are **more common**. Over many generations the population changes: that is **evolution by natural selection**, the idea Charles Darwin published in **1859**.

**The peppered moth is the classic case.** It rests on tree trunks by day, and its pale, speckled wings match the lichen on the bark, hiding it from the birds that eat it. A **dark** form, from a different allele, was first recorded in Manchester in **1848**. Then soot from factories blackened the trees and killed the lichen. On dark bark the pale moths were the visible ones, and birds ate them; the dark moths were hidden and survived to breed. By **1895**, **98%** of the peppered moths in Manchester were dark: only two in a hundred were pale.

**The moths did not change colour.** Both forms had always been there. What changed was **which form survived** to pass on its allele, and that is the whole idea in one sentence.

**The story reverses.** After the Clean Air Act of **1956** the soot went, the lichen returned, and pale moths became the hidden ones again. In clean woods today the pale form is back in the majority. The environment selects; change the environment and the selection changes with it.

steps.title: Extinction and biodiversity
steps.body:
Natural selection works only if the population contains the right variation and the environment changes slowly enough for selection to act over generations. When it does not, a species goes **extinct**: no members of it are left alive anywhere.

**What causes extinction:** a change in the environment, such as climate; a **new predator** or **competitor**, often brought by people; a **new disease**; **hunting**; and above all today the **loss of habitat** as forests are cleared and wetlands drained. The dodo, a flightless bird on an island with no predators, was gone within decades of sailors and their dogs and rats arriving, because nothing in its variation prepared it for either.

**Biodiversity** is the variety of living things in a place, or on Earth. It matters for reasons that are practical as well as moral: ecosystems with many species survive shocks better, many medicines come from plants and fungi, and crops need wild relatives whose genes can be bred in when a new disease arrives. Every extinction removes genes that cannot be replaced.

**Gene banks** are the insurance. A **seed bank** stores seeds of wild and crop plants, dried and frozen, so that a species or a variety lost in the field can be grown again. Zoos keep breeding populations of animals that have almost gone from the wild, and store frozen sperm and eggs. None of this replaces a habitat; it keeps the genes in existence until one can be restored.

a fungus reaching a frog population
a species whose range gets too warm

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Selection acts on variation that already exists.** The commonest wrong answer in this topic is that organisms *change* to suit their environment: the moths turned dark, the giraffes stretched their necks. They did not. The variation was there first, from different alleles, and the environment decided which of it survived to breed. A grade 9 answer always has the variation before the selection.

**The four steps are one argument.** Variation, competition, survival of the suited, alleles passed on: each step needs the one before. Leave out competition and there is no reason the less suited should die; leave out inheritance and the next generation is no different. Write all four, in order, whatever organism the question names.

**Species is about fertile offspring.** Lions and tigers share a genus and can produce a liger, but ligers are usually infertile, so the two remain separate species. The genus tells you they are close; the infertile hybrid tells you they are not the same.

**Why keys use structure, not colour or size.** A key must send every member of a species down the same branch. Legs, wings and shells do that; colour and size vary within a species and change with age, so they do not.

**Antibiotic resistance is the moth story in a hospital.** A population of bacteria varies; an antibiotic is the selection; the few with an allele that lets them survive it breed, and the population becomes resistant. It is the same four steps, running in days rather than decades, and it is why finishing a course matters.

**Extinction is selection with nothing to select.** If the environment changes faster than generations pass, or the population has no variation that suits the new conditions, selection cannot save it. That is why biodiversity, the variation across and within species, is the raw material of survival, and why gene banks store it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Classification** groups organisms by shared features. **Five kingdoms**: animals, plants, fungi, protists, prokaryotes (bacteria, no nucleus). Viruses are in none.
- The ranks: **kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**. Humans: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, *Homo*, *sapiens*.
- A **species**: members breed together to give **fertile** offspring. A mule is infertile, so horse and donkey are separate species.
- **Binomial names**, from Linnaeus in the 1750s: genus then species, *Homo sapiens*, *Panthera leo*. A shared genus means close relatives.
- A **dichotomous key** asks two-way questions about features that do not vary, such as legs and wings, never colour or size.
- An **adaptation** helps survival and reproduction in a habitat; **structural** (fur, spines) or **behavioural** (burrowing). Name the feature, what it does, why it helps there.
- **Natural selection**: variation, competition, survival of the best suited, alleles passed on. Darwin, **1859**.
- **Peppered moth**: dark form recorded **1848**; on sooty bark pale moths were eaten; **98%** dark in Manchester by **1895**; reversed after the **1956** Clean Air Act. The moths did not change; the proportion did.
- **Extinction** when the environment changes faster than selection can act: habitat loss, new predators, hunting, disease, climate. **Biodiversity** is the variation that survival depends on; **gene banks** store seeds, sperm and eggs.

Natural selection only works on animals that can move away, and a plant is rooted to the spot it grows in

questions.prompt: Explain how the peppered moth population in Manchester came to be 98% dark by 1895, and what happened after the Clean Air Act of 1956.
questions.solution:
The peppered moth rests on tree trunks by day, and its pale, speckled wings match the lichen on clean bark, hiding it from the birds that hunt it by sight. The population **varied**: a **dark form**, produced by a different allele, was first recorded in Manchester in **1848**, when it was rare, because on lichen-covered bark a dark moth stood out and was eaten.

Then the factories changed the environment. **Soot** blackened the tree trunks and killed the lichen. On dark bark the situation reversed: the **pale** moths were now the visible ones, and birds ate them, while the **dark** moths were hidden and **survived**. The moths that survived were the ones that **bred**, and they passed the **dark allele** to their offspring. Generation by generation the proportion of dark moths rose, until by **1895** they were **98%** of the Manchester population, only two in a hundred still pale.

No moth changed colour. Both forms had been there all along; what changed was **which form the birds could see**, and so which form lived to reproduce. That is natural selection: variation, competition, survival of the best suited, and the suited alleles passed on.

After the **Clean Air Act of 1956** the soot stopped, the bark cleaned and the lichen grew back. Now the dark moths were the visible ones and the pale moths were hidden, so the selection ran the other way: pale moths survived and bred, and in clean woods the pale form is back in the majority. The reversal is the strongest evidence in the story, because it shows the environment doing the choosing.

questions.prompt: A council must decide whether to spend money saving a rare plant that grows only on one local hillside. Evaluate the case for saving it, using the ideas of biodiversity, extinction and gene banks.
questions.solution:
A plant that grows on **one hillside** is one change away from **extinction**. If the hillside is built on, grazed bare or its climate shifts, there is no second population to fall back on, and a small population has little **variation** for natural selection to work with; selection can only choose among alleles that already exist, and it needs generations to act. So the question is not whether the plant will adapt on its own. It will not. The decision is whether it is worth keeping.

The case for keeping it rests on **biodiversity**. Ecosystems with more species survive shocks, such as a drought or a new disease, better than ecosystems with few, because different species fail under different conditions. Plants are a source of **medicines**, and most have never been tested. Wild plants carry **genes** that crop breeders need when a new pest or disease arrives, and a rare species may be the only source of a useful allele. Every extinction removes genes that **cannot be replaced**, and nobody knows in advance which ones will matter.

A **seed bank** is the cheap part of the answer: collect seed from the hillside, dry and freeze it, and the plant's genes survive whatever happens to the site. But a gene bank is insurance, not a solution. It keeps the genes **in existence**; it does not keep the plant growing, pollinated by its insects, feeding whatever eats it, and evolving as its habitat changes. Only **protecting the hillside** does that.

So the judgement is that the plant is worth saving, and that the two measures are not alternatives. Bank the seed now, because it is cheap and cannot be done after the plant is gone; then protect the hillside, because the seed bank only buys time. Against a one-off cost, the council is weighing a species that took millions of years to evolve and can never be made again.

examTechnique.body:
The marks in this topic are for **order** and for **mechanism**. Order: the seven ranks, and the four steps of natural selection, each written in sequence. Mechanism: not *the moths adapted* but *the pale ones were visible and eaten, the dark ones survived and bred, and the dark allele spread*. Whatever organism a question names, the four steps are the same, so learn them as a template and fill in the details.

For adaptation, write three parts every time: the feature, what it does, why it helps in that habitat. For a species question, the word is *fertile*. For a key, the features are structures, not colours. And never let an organism *change itself*: variation comes first, and the environment chooses.
examinerErrors: Saying organisms **changed to suit** their environment. The variation existed first; selection changed the **proportion**.
Leaving a step out of natural selection, usually **competition** or **passing on the alleles**.
Defining a species as animals that can breed, without **fertile** offspring. Horse and donkey can breed; the mule cannot.
Writing the binomial name with the genus in lower case or the species with a capital, or putting them the wrong way round.
Giving a feature without its function and its **link to the habitat**: *thick fur* alone.
Building a key on **colour** or **size**, which vary within a species.
Putting viruses into a kingdom, or bacteria among the protists. Bacteria are **prokaryotes**; viruses are in **no kingdom**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer runs natural selection as a template, four steps in order, with variation before anything else, and applies it unprompted to a case it has never seen: a finch, a bacterium, a weed that survives the weedkiller. It writes an adaptation as feature, function and habitat, and reads an unfamiliar animal's adaptations from a description. It uses the species definition to settle a lion-and-tiger question with the word *fertile*, knows why a shared genus matters, and can say why a key is built on structure. It sees the peppered moth's reversal after 1956 as the strongest evidence, because the environment changed and the selection changed with it, and it sees antibiotic resistance as the same story with a different bird.
